title: Temiya the silent prince
hook: a prince pretends to be mute for sixteen years rather than rule by punishment

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vessantara's children, and the argument Buddhists have had about them for centuries. Your line was the tradition argues too. Did you ask one hard question out loud? Day ninety-four.

Think of a meeting where you stayed quiet. Maybe it was wisdom. Maybe it was fear. From the outside, the two look exactly the same. Nobody can see why you didn't speak. Today's story is about a silence so long and so stubborn that everyone decided the silent one was broken. He wasn't. He was choosing. It's the Temiya Jataka, number 538, the first of the ten long Jatakas that close the collection, and it starts with a baby on a king's lap.
screen: `WISDOM OR FEAR?` → `FROM OUTSIDE, THEY LOOK THE SAME.` → `A BABY ON A KING'S LAP.`

segments.voice: The baby is Temiya, the long-awaited son of the king of Benares. One day, still only an infant, he's sitting on his father's lap while the king judges prisoners, and he watches his father order terrible punishments. And the story says the baby remembers: in a past life he was a king too, and the harsh judgments he handed down led him to long suffering afterward. He's terrified. He does not want this throne. A goddess who lives in the royal parasol gives him advice: pretend you can't speak, can't hear, can't walk. So he does. For sixteen years. The court tries everything to catch him out. Sweets he could reach for. Frightening noises. Fire. Snakes. Every test, the story says, he stays still. Finally the advisers tell the king this son is bad luck, and the king orders him taken out and buried. The charioteer drives him to the forest and starts to dig. And then Temiya stands up, walks, lifts the chariot, and speaks. He tells the charioteer why he kept silent, and he chooses the life of a forest ascetic. In the end his parents and much of the kingdom come out and follow him. In the tradition, this life is linked with nekkhamma, renunciation: leaving behind the power that would have made him cruel. And notice what his silence was. Not weakness. Not sulking. A refusal. He would not say the words that condemn. Sometimes the strongest thing a person does is decline to join in.
screen: `THE BABY SEES THE PUNISHMENTS.` · `SIXTEEN YEARS WITHOUT A WORD.` · `HE STANDS, AND SPEAKS.` · `A SILENCE THAT REFUSES.` · then, large: `SILENCE CAN BE A CHOICE.`

segments.voice: For the sit, simply be silent on purpose. Settle, and notice how much talking happens in your head: replies, rehearsals, arguments with people who aren't here. You don't need to stop them. Just decline to follow them. When a sentence starts forming, notice it, and let it go unsaid, like Temiya on his father's lap. Then come back to the breath. Later today, if you can, try ten minutes with no speaking, no typing, no scrolling. The bell holds the time.
Temiya the silent prince. The prince who kept silent for sixteen years rather than rule by punishment.
Your line: silence can be a choice. Today, keep ten minutes of real silence, and once, choose not to join a pile-on. Day ninety-four.

howItsDone: The Temiya story is told as the first of the ten great Jatakas, and in Thailand and elsewhere it's painted on temple walls; Buddhists link it with the perfection of renunciation.

fork.setup: you're Temiya, sixteen years silent, and the charioteer is digging your grave. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he stands, lifts the chariot, and tells the charioteer why. then he chooses the forest, not the throne.

original.note: Pali: renunciation, the perfection the tradition links with Temiya's life.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prince who wouldn't talk.
what it means: a chosen silence that refuses to join in cruelty, and turns toward renunciation.
what a scholar hears: the Pali title is Mugapakkha Jataka, the story of the one who seemed mute and lame; it opens the ten great births, each linked by the tradition to one perfection.

notes: Plot details (the infant on the king's lap, the past life as a king followed by suffering in hell, the goddess of the parasol, the tests, the charioteer Sunanda, lifting the chariot) are paraphrased; confirm against Jataka 538.
